This tutorial provides a brief overview of options for plotting results, printing objects, and saving results.

## Global plotting configuration

HPVsim allows the user to set various options that apply to all plots. You can change the font size, default DPI, whether plots should be shown by default, etc. (for the full list, see `hpv.options.help()`). For example, we might want higher resolution, to turn off automatic figure display, close figures after they're rendered, and to turn off the messages that print when a simulation is running. We can do this using built-in defaults for Jupyter notebooks (and then run a sim) with:

```{python}
import hpvsim as hpv

hpv.options(jupyter=True, verbose=0) # Standard options for Jupyter notebook

sim = hpv.Sim()
sim.run()
```

## Printing objects

You can get a summary of a sim with `summarize()`:

```{python}
sim.summarize()
```

To show the full object, including all methods and attributes, use `disp()`:

```{python}
sim.disp()
```

## Plotting options

While a sim can be plotted using default settings simply by `sim.plot()`, this is just a small fraction of what's available. First, note that results can be plotted directly using e.g. Matplotlib. Results are organized by module: you can see the top-level keys with `sim.results.keys()`, and each disease genotype (e.g. `hpv16`) and the aggregate `hpvtotal` view has its own set of results. The shared time axis is `sim.results.timevec`. A simple example of plotting using Matplotlib is:

```{python}
import pylab as plt # Shortcut for import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot(sim.results.timevec, sim.results.hpvtotal.cum_infections);
```

Each result is a `Result` object rather than a plain NumPy array; like a pandas column, you can get the underlying array via slicing (`sim.results.hpvtotal.cum_infections[:]`) or the `.values` attribute.

The built-in `sim.plot()` produces a multi-panel overview of the key results:

```{python}
sim.plot();
```

We can save the resulting figure using Matplotlib's `savefig()`. `sim.plot()` returns the figure object, so:

```{python}
fig = sim.plot()
fig.savefig('my-fig.png', dpi=150)
```

## Customizing plots

We saw above how to set default plot configuration options for Jupyter. HPVsim provides a lot of flexibility in customizing the appearance of plots as well. There are three different levels at which you can set plotting options: global, just for HPVsim, or just for the current plot. To give an example with changing the figure DPI:
- Change the setting globally (for both HPVsim and Matplotlib): `sc.options(dpi=150)` or `plt.rc('figure', dpi=150)` (where `sc` is `import sciris as sc`)
- Change for HPVsim plots, but not for Matplotlib plots: `hpv.options(dpi=150)`
- Change for the current HPVsim plot, but not other HPVsim plots: `sim.plot(dpi=150)`

The easiest way to change the style of HPVsim plots is with the `style` argument. For example, to plot using a built-in Matplotlib style would simply be:

```{python}
sim.plot(style='ggplot');
```

In addition to the default style (`'hpvsim'`), there is also a "simple" style:

```{python}
sim.plot(style='simple');
```

Although most style handling is done automatically, you can also use it yourself in a with block, e.g.:

```{python}
import numpy as np
with hpv.options.with_style(fontsize=6):
    sim.plot() # This will have 6 point font
    plt.figure(); plt.plot(np.random.rand(20), 'o') # So will this
```

## Saving options

Saving sims is also pretty simple. The simplest way to save is simply

```{python}
sim.save('my-sim.sim')
```

Technically, this saves as a gzipped pickle file (via `sc.save()` from the Sciris library). Before writing, `save()` shrinks the sim — freeing the random-number generators and internal back-references — so the file stays small; the reloaded sim is ready to inspect. For example, here's what it would look like to create a sim, run it partway, save it, load it, and finish running it:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

sim_orig = hpv.Sim(start=2000, stop=2030, label='Load & save example')
sim_orig.run(until=2015)
sim_orig.save('my-half-finished-sim.sim')

sim = ss.load('my-half-finished-sim.sim')
sim.run()
sim.plot();
```

Aside from saving the entire simulation, you can also work with the results directly. The results arrays share the `sim.results.timevec` time axis, so it is straightforward to assemble them into a pandas DataFrame for storage or further processing:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    'year': sim.results.timevec,
    'cum_infections': sim.results.hpvtotal.cum_infections[:],
    'new_cancers': sim.results.hpvtotal.new_cancers[:],
})
df.to_csv('my-sim.csv', index=False)
print(df.head())
```
